title: Loving strangers
hook: in several traditions, the stranger is a test of love

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving children. Your line was through you, not from you. Did a child get to be themselves about one thing, with no correction? Today, love goes out past the family to people with no names at all. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

Who was the last stranger to do something kind for you? Someone who held a door with a foot while juggling groceries. A driver who waved you into traffic. A person on a train who pointed out that your bag was open. They'll probably never turn up again, and they didn't need anything back. Strangers are the people love has the least reason to reach: no history, no debt, no family tie. That's exactly why several ancient texts made the stranger a test. Today: a tent in the desert, a law about memory, a line about angels, and a princess in Homer.
screen: `THE LAST STRANGER WHO WAS KIND.` → `NO HISTORY, NO DEBT.` → `WHY THE STRANGER IS A TEST.`

segments.voice: First, Abraham runs to the strangers. In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he looks up and sees three men standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows, and asks them to stay. Then he hurries: water for their feet, fresh bread, a calf prepared, food set before them while he stands by. The chapter opens by telling the reader that the LORD appeared to Abraham there; how much Abraham himself understood at first, the text leaves open. Second, ye were strangers. The law in Leviticus doesn't just say tolerate the outsider. It says: "thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason given is memory. You know what it's like to be the outsider, so love the outsider. Third, angels unawares. The letter to the Hebrews, in the New Testament, has a single line in which some readers hear Abraham's story: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The stranger at the door might be more than they seem. The Greeks had their own version: in Homer's Odyssey, a princess tells her frightened friends that strangers and beggars come from Zeus. Fourth, a smile is small hospitality. Not everyone has a tent or a calf to offer. But hospitality comes in small sizes: eye contact with the cashier, patience with a lost tourist, a nod to the new person at work. These texts treat the stranger not as a risk to manage but as someone to welcome, while still using common sense about safety. In these texts, the stranger is where love reaches past loyalty.
screen: `ABRAHAM RUNS TO THE STRANGERS.` · `YE WERE STRANGERS.` · `ANGELS UNAWARES.` · `A SMILE IS SMALL HOSPITALITY.` · then, large: `THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and let the day's strangers come back to mind: a face on the street, a voice on the phone, someone in a waiting room. Then go further back, to a stranger who once did something kind for you: a door held, a wave into traffic, directions on a strange street. Stay with that moment for a few breaths and let the thanks you never got to say be said silently now. Then look ahead to today's route. Where will you meet someone you don't know: a counter, a bus, a doorway? Choose the place, and the small courtesy you'll offer there. If you pray, you can give thanks for that stranger before God, nameless as they are. The bell holds the time.
Loving strangers. Welcome offered to people with no claim on you, the way Abraham ran to his guests and Leviticus says to love the outsider as yourself. Today's word.
Your line: the stranger. Today, smile at one stranger on purpose, or offer one small courtesy, and expect nothing back. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Abraham's welcome of three guests in Genesis 18 as a model of hospitality, and the Torah commands love for the stranger; hospitality to guests and travelers is also honored in other faiths and cultures.

what it means: welcoming the outsider, with no claim on you, as a real act of love.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear Genesis 18 behind Hebrews 13:2, and Leviticus 19:34 grounds love for the stranger in Israel's own memory of Egypt.

notes: Audit pass (serious): Genesis 18:1 tells the reader at the outset that 'the LORD appeared unto him', so 'only later does the story reveal who his guests were' was wrong, and the myth/fork claimed Abraham acted 'before he knows', which the text does not say (readers differ on what Abraham recognized, e.g. his 'My Lord' in 18:3). Teach, myth and fork reveal corrected; the narrator's closing verdict on what love 'really' is was softened.
The outline hook ('the stranger is the oldest test in many traditions') is softened to 'several traditions' and 'oldest' is dropped under the claims rule.
Odyssey 6: Nausicaa tells her maids that strangers and beggars come from Zeus; paraphrased, no translation quoted.
Hebrews 13:2 echoing Genesis 18 is a common reading, not stated in the text itself; the script says 'some readers hear Abraham's story' in it.
howItsDone: 'also honored in other faiths and cultures' is a general claim with no cited source; confirm or cut.
φιλοξενία: confirm the accent and pronunciation.
